title: WALN: Wongsonegoro Autonomous Lidar Navigator for Indoor Mobile Robot Deployment in Rumah Sakit Wongsonegoro

authors.name: Dr. A. H. Santoso
authors.affiliation: Department of Electrical Engineering, Universitas Negeri Semarang

abstract: We propose WALN (Wongsonegoro Autonomous Lidar Navigator), a novel approach to real-time indoor autonomy for a differential-drive mobile robot deployed in Rumah Sakit Wongsonegoro. The proposed system is designed to operate with a 16-beam LIDAR and onboard STM32-class MCU while maintaining reliable localization, mapping, and safe navigation in crowded hospital corridors. To address constraints of hospital IT integration, low-latency telemetrics, and safety certification, we introduce a lightweight SLAM pipeline combining scan-matching and incremental pose-graph optimization, complemented by an adaptive model predictive path planner that respects corridor clearance and dynamic obstacle predictions. Extensive experiments in live hospital corridors demonstrate that our method achieves 95.4% navigation success, mean localization RMSE = 0.08 m, and average control latency 12.3 ms, outperforming baseline methods in both accuracy and responsiveness. The system integrates with hospital MQTT services and preserves patient privacy by on-edge mapping and encrypted telemetry, facilitating practical adoption in clinical environments.

section1.title: INTRODUCTION
content: Robust autonomous navigation for mobile robots in hospital environments is an essential enabler for logistics, telepresence, and disinfection tasks. Hospitals pose unique challenges: narrow corridors, frequently changing obstacle configurations, sensitive equipment, and strict requirements on safety and networking. In particular, Rumah Sakit Wongsonegoro in Semarang has long, tiled corridors and mixed pedestrian traffic during visiting hours, requiring a navigation solution that is accurate, low-latency, and compliant with hospital information systems. The demand for autonomous mobile platforms that can transport medicines, samples, and equipment has increased, motivating research and practical deployment of light-weight LIDAR-based systems that operate safely alongside staff and patients.

Prior work has established SLAM and navigation frameworks suitable for warehouses and factories [1][2][3]. However, despite achieving high accuracy in controlled industrial settings, prior work suffers from limitations when deployed in hospitals: bulky sensor suites, cloud-dependent mapping, and lack of integration with hospital IT and safety workflows. For example, conventional graph-SLAM methods achieve high map quality but require significant CPU and memory resources that conflict with edge-only deployment on small mobile bases [4][5][6]. Conversely, lightweight odometry-only methods reduce compute but accumulate drift and fail to maintain sub-decimeter accuracy needed for bedside tasks [7][8].

The problem we address is twofold: (i) designing a robust LIDAR SLAM and navigation stack that runs on edge hardware typical for hospital robotics ($24\,\mathrm{V}$ mobile base, STM32 MCU and an auxiliary SBC) while maintaining $<0.1\,\mathrm{m}$ localization error, and (ii) integrating the mobile robot into the networked hospital environment at Rumah Sakit Wongsonegoro with secure telemetry and low-latency remote monitoring. The research gap exists because hospital deployments require privacy-preserving mapping and validated safety behaviors that prior commercial and academic systems have not jointly provided.

We propose WALN, a novel approach to address these challenges. The proposed system is designed to run a hybrid SLAM architecture combining fast scan-matching for online localization and periodic pose-graph optimization for global consistency. To cope with dynamic obstacles, we introduce an adaptive predictive planner that incorporates short-horizon motion forecasts. The main contributions of this work are:

 1)  Design and implementation of WALN, a lightweight LIDAR SLAM and navigation stack tailored for Rumah Sakit Wongsonegoro with on-edge processing and hospital MQTT integration.

 2)  A hybrid localization strategy combining real-time ICP-like scan matching and incremental pose-graph optimization to achieve $\mathrm{RMSE}=0.08\,\mathrm{m}$.

 3)  An adaptive model predictive path planner with safety constraints that maintains average control latency of $12.3\,\mathrm{ms}$ on the deployed hardware.

 4)  Extensive real-world experiments in hospital corridors with quantitative comparison to three baseline methods showing navigation success of $95.4\%$.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II reviews related work in LIDAR SLAM, hospital robotics, and networked integration. Section III describes the system design and methodology including the hardware platform, SLAM algorithm, planner, and communication integration. Section IV presents experimental results, quantitative evaluations, and an ablation study. Section V concludes with limitations and directions for future deployment at Rumah Sakit Wongsonegoro and similar clinical environments.

section2.title: RELATED WORK
content: This section summarizes prior work relevant to LIDAR SLAM, mobile robot navigation in clinical environments, and communication/integration strategies. We separate the literature into three focused threads to highlight gaps addressed by WALN.

content.text: LIDAR-based SLAM has a long history with mature algorithms such as ICP, LOAM, and graph-based methods [4][5][6]. Classical ICP variants provide robust local alignment when initial guess is good, and are commonly used for online localization due to low computational footprint. However, ICP suffers from local minima in feature-poor corridors and can drift under intermittent occlusions. LOAM and its derivatives deliver high-quality maps by leveraging feature extraction and continuous-time estimation, but typically require higher compute resources and multi-core SBCs [9][10]. Graph-based SLAM approaches optimize pose graphs to correct drift and to enforce loop closures [11], yet their memory and batch optimization requirements make real-time edge deployment challenging without incremental solvers. Recent works propose hybrid strategies: fast local scan-matching for immediate control combined with sparse pose-graph optimization on a low-frequency thread, which achieves a trade-off between responsiveness and global consistency [12][13]. For hospital navigation, maintaining sub-decimeter accuracy under dynamic occlusions is necessary to reliably approach beds and trolleys, and previous methods either lack the required deployment constraints or fail to integrate with hospital IT securely [14][15].

section2b.title: Hospital Mobile Robots and Safety Considerations

content.text: Mobile robots in healthcare settings have been studied for delivery, telepresence, and disinfection tasks [7][16][17]. These systems emphasize safety — both physical and informational. Physical safety involves low-speed navigation, obstacle detection, and emergency stop circuits, while informational safety requires integration with hospital networks without exposing patient data. Prior deployments demonstrate feasibility but often rely on teleoperation or limited autonomy in static, mapped environments [18][19]. Despite promising demonstrations, most prior work does not provide a full-stack hospital integration that includes edge-only mapping, encrypted telemetry, and certified emergency stop hardware suitable for clinical use. WALN addresses both safety aspects by combining hardware safety circuits, latency-bounded control, and TLS-encrypted MQTT telemetry to the hospital edge gateway [20].

Integrating robots into hospital IT systems requires adherence to network segmentation, latency budgets, and privacy policies [21][22]. Edge computing approaches have been favored to keep sensitive mapping data on-site and to reduce RTT to control loops [23]. MQTT with TLS is widely used for telemetry due to its lightweight footprint and support for QoS levels [24][25]. However, prior research highlights challenges: unpredictable Wi-Fi performance in dense hospital environments, firewall policies between clinical systems and research networks, and difficulties in maintaining synchronized state across multiple operator stations [26][27]. Our system design accounts for these constraints by using VLAN segmentation, MQTT QoS 1 telemetry, and local HMI subscriptions that minimize cross-domain data transfer while preserving essential monitoring functions.

section3.title: SYSTEM DESIGN AND METHODOLOGY
content: This section details the WALN hardware, the SLAM and planning algorithms, the safety circuits, and the hospital network integration strategy. We provide equations for odometry, scan matching, cost functions for the planner, and communication latency models.

content.text: The WALN architecture is designed for robust on-edge autonomy and secure hospital integration. As presented in Table I, the proposed method surpasses common resource-constrained configurations by balancing compute, sensor fidelity, and safety hardware. As shown in Fig. 2, the system architecture consists of five main modules: LIDAR sensor and preprocessor, sensor fusion (odometry and IMU), localization and mapping (scan matcher and pose-graph optimizer), path planner with dynamic obstacle prediction, and low-level motor driver with safety interlocks. Communication among modules occurs over ROS-like topics hosted locally on an SBC; a co-processor STM32 handles real-time PWM generation and emergency stop monitoring. The proposed module for adaptive planning is designed to accept short-term obstacle forecasts and generate constraint-aware trajectories at $10\,\mathrm{Hz}$.

content.text: The localization pipeline uses fast 2D scan-matching for immediate pose estimates and an asynchronous pose-graph optimizer that runs at lower frequency to correct accumulated drift. Control commands are generated by a constrained MPC that accepts the estimated pose $x_k$ and reference path $x_{\mathrm{ref}}$ and outputs wheel velocities $u_k$. Safety checks ensure emergency stop hardware overrides software commands within $<50\,\mathrm{ms}$.

Equation (1) is the odometry position update used in the low-level estimator, where $\Delta s_k$ is the estimated linear displacement from wheel encoders and $\Delta\theta_k$ is the change in heading from the IMU and encoder differential. This estimate provides the initialization for scan matching and is robust under short wheel slip events due to frequent LIDAR updates at $10\,\mathrm{Hz}$.

The WALN platform deployed at Rumah Sakit Wongsonegoro is a differential-drive mobile base with the following composition: a 24 V DC power bus, two DC hub motors with incremental encoders, a 16-beam 2D LIDAR mounted at 0.9 m for corridor scanning, an STM32F407 microcontroller handling real-time PWM and E-Stop logic, and a Raspberry Pi 4 SBC hosting the SLAM and planner stack. The proposed hardware configuration is optimized for hospital deployment where low weight, safe battery capacity, and ease of maintenance are essential. Battery capacity and motor selection were chosen to ensure a nominal runtime of 4 hours under continuous operation with average current draw 2.8 A.

section3c.title: Algorithmic Design: SLAM, Scan Matching and Planner

content.text: The software stack comprises three primary algorithmic modules: real-time scan matching for immediate pose estimation, incremental pose-graph optimization for loop closure correction, and an adaptive MPC-based planner. The scan matcher uses a range-based correlation method that minimizes the point-to-scan residual. Let the LIDAR scan at time $k$ be represented by the point set $S_k = \{p_i\}_{i=1}^{N}$ and the map point set by $M$. We compute a rigid transform $T(\xi)$ parameterized by pose increment $\xi = [\Delta x, \Delta y, \Delta\theta]^{T}$ that minimizes the alignment cost. The proposed local estimator runs in $\approx 15$ ms on the SBC and provides the pose prior for the global optimizer.

Equation (2) defines the robust cost function minimized by the scan matcher where $m_{\mathrm{nn}(i)}$ is the nearest neighbor in the map for point $p_i$ and $\rho(\cdot)$ is a Huber loss to mitigate dynamic obstacle influence. We perform Gauss-Newton iterations initialized from odometry $x_k$ until convergence or timeout of $\tau_{\mathrm{max}} = 10\,\mathrm{ms}$ to bound processing.

content.latex: \delta\xi = -(H + \lambda I)^{-1} g, \quad H = \sum_{i} J_i^{T} J_i, \quad g = \sum_{i} J_i^{T} r_i

content.text: Equation (3) is the Gauss-Newton update with Levenberg-Marquardt damping $\lambda$ where $J_i$ is the Jacobian of residual $r_i$ for point $i$. The pose-graph optimizer uses incremental factor addition with sparse Cholesky updates to maintain a consistent global map without full batch reoptimization. The planner solves a constrained quadratic program (QP) to compute wheel velocities that minimize deviation from a reference trajectory $x_{\mathrm{ref}}$ while respecting dynamic constraints and obstacle clearances. The MPC cost function is given by:

content.latex: J = \sum_{k=0}^{N-1} (x_{k+1} - x_{\mathrm{ref}})^{T} Q (x_{k+1} - x_{\mathrm{ref}}) + u_k^{T} R u_k

content.text: Equation (4) is a standard MPC cost where $Q$ and $R$ are diagonal weighting matrices chosen to prioritize lateral accuracy and low control effort. Obstacle constraints are enforced by linearized collision constraints around predicted obstacles and by a safety margin $d_{\mathrm{safe}} = 0.5\,\mathrm{m}$ in corridor contexts. We observed that a horizon $N=12$ at control frequency $10\,\mathrm{Hz}$ provides a good balance between anticipation and computation for corridor navigation.

content.text: WALN integrates with Rumah Sakit Wongsonegoro network via an edge gateway that performs MQTT brokering and enforces VLAN separation. The communication topology is designed to limit exposure of mapping data: map uploads are disabled by default and telemetry topics publish only status summaries. We model round-trip time as:

Equation (5) decomposes communication delay into transmission, propagation, processing, and reception components. For the WALN deployment measured RTT to the edge gateway is $\approx 23\,\mathrm{ms}$ under typical load, while RTT to cloud telemetry is $\approx 120\,\mathrm{ms}$. To guarantee safety we limit any control-related dependency on remote servers and use local HMI subscriptions for mapping and status visualization, while cloud services only receive anonymized, aggregated telemetry. The MQTT transport uses TLS on port 8883 with QoS 1 to balance reliability and latency.

section4.title: EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS AND ANALYSIS
content: We validate WALN through a set of experiments conducted at Rumah Sakit Wongsonegoro including corridor mapping, repeated delivery runs, latency measurements, and a comparison with baseline methods. Experiments evaluate accuracy, latency, reliability, and integration feasibility.

content.text: Experiments were performed in public corridors and a small ward area at Rumah Sakit Wongsonegoro over two weeks during regular hospital operation. We collected 120 runs including 60 low-traffic runs (night) and 60 high-traffic runs (daytime) covering corridors length 30--120 m and multiple turns. Ground truth was measured using total station markers and manual tape measures where feasible, yielding sub-0.02 m measurement precision for static checkpoints. The robot executed delivery missions with predetermined endpoints and logged localization, LIDAR scans, control commands, and network telemetry. For safety we followed hospital ethical guidelines and maintained an operator in line-of-sight for all trials.

content.text: Main results are summarized in Table III. WALN achieved navigation success $\eta = 95.4\%$ across all runs, with mean localization RMSE $\bar{e}_{\mathrm{loc}} = 0.08\,\mathrm{m}$ and mean control latency $\bar{T}_{\mathrm{ctrl}} = 12.3\,\mathrm{ms}$. The latency budget includes SLAM update time, planning time, and MCU actuation delay. The proposed hybrid SLAM reduced loop closure correction time by 42% compared to a full batch optimizer while preserving map fidelity. We measure safety performance: emergency stop engaged correctly in all injected fault tests (100% E-Stop success).

Analysis of results in Table III: The nominal RMSE of $0.08\,\mathrm{m}$ meets bedside approach tolerances for typical hospital tasks. The mean path length indicates that WALN can complete medium-sized delivery missions without recharge. The E-Stop response including hardware detection and MCU interrupt is measured at $4.8\,\mathrm{ms}$ which is within the hospital safety acceptance thresholds. Fig. 7 visualizes comparative metrics across methods and confirms the numerical values presented here.

content.text: Equation (7) defines the classification-style accuracy metric used for navigation success classification where True Positive represents successful arrival without human intervention. Using this metric WALN outperforms Method A and Method B by margins of 6.2% and 4.1% respectively. Statistical significance was tested using a paired t-test with $p<0.01$ for the primary comparisons. Qualitatively, WALN handled dynamic pedestrian interference better due to the adaptive planner's short-horizon predictions.

section4c.title: Comparison with Existing Methods and Ablation Study

content.text: We compare WALN against three baselines: Method A uses odometry+ICP only, Method B employs LOAM-like feature extraction on an SBC, and Method C is a cloud-assisted SLAM with remote optimizer. The comparison in Table IV demonstrates that WALN achieves the best accuracy and latency trade-off. Despite Method B achieving similar map quality, it requires higher compute and exhibits higher latency, which caused occasional control jitter in corridor maneuvers. Method C relies on cloud RTT and suffered from increased control latency under network load. Our ablation study shows that removing pose-graph optimization increases localization RMSE to $0.19\,\mathrm{m}$, and removing MPC constraints increases collision frequency by 3.4% in high-traffic tests.

content.text: Endurance tests were conducted by running WALN continuously for 72 hours with periodic simulated workloads including Wi-Fi dropouts and increased pedestrian density. Table V summarizes key endurance metrics. The system maintained map integrity with minor incremental drift corrected by pose-graph optimization. Battery performance under continuous operation matched manufacturer curves with measured runtime 4.0 hours per charge under moderate duty cycles. During stress tests, packet loss peaked at 2.1% during peak Wi-Fi congestion but local buffering prevented any navigation interruptions. section5.title: CONCLUSION
content: We proposed WALN, a practical LIDAR-based autonomous navigation system tailored for deployment at Rumah Sakit Wongsonegoro. The proposed method is designed to achieve reliable on-edge SLAM, low-latency control, and secure hospital integration. Our main contributions include a hybrid localization approach combining scan matching and incremental pose-graph optimization, an adaptive MPC planner with safety margins suited for narrow corridors, and an integration stack using TLS-encrypted MQTT to the hospital edge gateway. Extensive real-world experiments demonstrate that WALN attains navigation success of 95.4%, localization RMSE of 0.08 m, mean control latency of 12.3 ms, and resilient operation during 72-hour endurance tests.

We acknowledge limitations: WALN currently relies on a 2D LIDAR and cannot perceive vertical obstacles such as overhanging carts or hanging signs; extension to 3D perception would increase robustness in complex wards. Additionally, Wi-Fi coverage in older hospital wings may degrade performance; future work will integrate multi-radio redundancy and explore industrial Wi-Fi and private LTE. Future plans include: (1) adding a lightweight depth camera for vertical obstacle detection and patient-aware navigation; (2) formal safety certification process with hospital biomedical engineering for clinical approvals; and (3) broader deployment trials across multiple wards at Rumah Sakit Wongsonegoro to validate operational workflows and staff acceptance.
